newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Indonesia rejects any EU aid direct to Timor.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia rejects any EU aid direct to Timor.

text.p: Indonesia on Friday firmly rejected any attempt by the European Union, under pressure from Portugal to take a stronger line on East Timor, to provide humanitarian help directly to the disputed territory.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told a news conference at the World Economic Forum that such a move would be unacceptable, as the former Portuguese colony formed part of Indonesia and any aid programmes would have to be channelled through Jakarta.
The EU proposed at a summit last month to send aid to Timor for such projects as building primary schools.

"We cannot accept that (direct aid)," said the minister, who is due to meet United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan in Davos on Saturday to discuss stalled talks between Lisbon and Indonesia over the future of the territory.

The periodic and largely unfruitful talks have been held under U.N. auspices but the last scheduled meeting between Alatas and his Portuguese counterpart Jaime Gama was called off in December because of the change of leadership at the United Nations.
Annan replaced Boutros Boutros Ghali as secretary-general in December.
Indonesia invaded the territory in 1975, shortly after the Portuguese left, and formally annexed it in 1976 but the move has never been recognised by the United Nations.

The question of the future of the territory, in the Timor Sea some 500 km (300 miles) north of Australia, has become a thorn in the side of relations between the European Union and Asian countries, particularly the seven-country ASEAN trade block of which Indonesia is a member.
Alatas said that he would have no new proposals to put to Annan about Timor. He said that the two men would discuss how the talks with Portugal should proceed and at what level.
